subject: hedgehog
pitch: A plump hedgehog out on an autumn evening walk. A dome of spines in chestnut brown with cream tips, a soft fawn face with a pointed, twitchy snout, a shiny black button nose, tiny round ears and bright beady eyes. Little pink paws, and a single red maple leaf stuck on its spines like a trophy.
reasoning:
I need to stick to only the documented SDK functions I can verify exist, so I'm restricting myself to the known builder methods and utilities rather than guessing at an unverified API surface.

My plan is a hedgehog built from a dome-shaped body with scattered spine geometry seated along the surface normals at each sampled point, using cone shapes for spines with lighter tips, oriented outward via the hit frame from surface scattering.

I'm sizing the body sphere realistically with a slight squash scale for a hedgehog proportion, then working out the joint hierarchy starting from a root hip/body joint near the ground for the head and limb chains.

For the head I'm planning a neck-to-head joint chain with a forward-pointing cone snout and a small nose sphere at its tip, then four simple leg joints (front/back, left/right) with capsule limbs ending in small pink paw spheres. For the leaf accessory I'm leaning toward building a proper THREE.Shape with a leaf-like outline and extruding it with THREE.ExtrudeGeometry rather than relying on an uncertain helper signature, since that gives more predictable control over the shape.

For the dorsal spines I'm thinking of using a surface scatter technique, sampling points around a body center with azimuth/elevation loops and some jitter, placing a chestnut cone base at each hit plus a smaller cream-colored tip cone offset slightly along the spine for a two-tone needle look.

For the rest of the anatomy I'm planning fawn-colored spheres for ears partially embedded at the head sides, black spheres for eyes with tiny white highlights, a black nose sphere at the snout tip, and a fawn head sphere positioned at the neck joint.

Now I'm figuring out the snout as a cone aimed along the +Z direction using the part's dir option, placing eyes, ears, and nose at specific offsets from the head, and setting up the legs as cylinders anchored at hip joints with pink paw spheres at the feet, using the bone option to attach parts to joints.

Setting up the skeleton, I'm defining the body, neck, and head joints with parent relationships, though I'm uncertain whether the module expects the parent name as a string or the joint object itself — I'll pass the joint object and hope it's accepted. For the legs, I'm placing joints in absolute model-space coordinates as required.

For the chestnut-colored dome body, I'm planning to cover it with spines using a surface-based placement system, looping through elevation and azimuth angles around the body center to scatter spines while leaving the face area bare — though I'm unsure whether the angles are expected in radians or degrees.

For a more reliable approach, I'm computing explicit points on the body ellipsoid using spherical coordinates scaled by the body's radii, then calling the surface's nearest-point function to anchor each spine precisely, skipping the frontal region to avoid covering the face. I'm aiming for roughly 7 rows by 16 columns of spines (about 110 total, each built from 2-3 parts), keeping the total part count comfortably under 1000, with cones using 6 radial segments for efficiency, and matching the body sphere's scale and position exactly to this ellipsoid so the spine placement lines up correctly.

Now I'm working out the exact geometry for each spine: a cone for the main chestnut-colored shaft translated so its base sits at the body surface, plus a smaller cream-colored cone layered near the tip to create a two-tone spine effect, adjusting the translation offsets so the tip segment overlaps slightly with the base segment for a seamless look.

Settling on a cream cone tip positioned atop the chestnut base, with the overall spine scaled up slightly for visibility since real hedgehog spines would be too small to read well at this scale. Now I'm thinking through how each spine attaches along the surface normal and planning to build a skin surface helper for finding nearest points, then moving on to sketching a simple maple-leaf shape using a sequence of points for an extruded outline.

I'm working out the rotation math to reorient the leaf's extrusion from the Z axis to the Y axis so it stands properly when seated, then translating it slightly upward so it floats above the spines rather than sitting buried at the base.

Now I'm picking the hit point for the leaf placement near the top-back of the body, then moving on to the eyes (black beady spheres with small white highlight dots), the ears (flattened ellipsoid spheres using scale options), and the snout (a fawn-colored scaled sphere topped with a forward-pointing cone for the muzzle).

I'm setting up the joint hierarchy for the head and legs, placing paw spheres (pink, flattened and elongated) at the end of each leg cylinder, then defining a seeded random generator for jitter and planning a loop over spherical rows/columns to scatter spines across the body.

For the body ellipsoid, I'm computing surface points from phi/theta angles while skipping the front-facing region (so spines don't cover the face) and the underside, then estimating total spine/part counts to keep the triangle budget under control, deciding spines will just follow the surface normal without extra backward tilt for simplicity.

I'm picking chestnut spine bases with cream tips, adding a fawn belly patch underneath the body, and planning the joint hierarchy (body root, neck, head) with legs parented to the body, each leg built from a cylinder plus a pink paw cylinder, keeping imports minimal to just the essentials.

I'm positioning ears as flattened fawn spheres on the sides of the head, a black nose at the snout tip, and eyes placed symmetrically on the face, then setting up the meta export with name and description before finding a surface point near the top of the body to stick the leaf, angled along the normal at that spot.
